final_answer: Short answer: it should not matter for the Guidelines range, so neither office has a Guidelines-based advantage; the practical choice turns on venue and statutory-maximum stacking, not on which district's judge sentences. Reasoning: (1) The Guidelines are a single national system. Section 1347 offenses are sentenced under USSG 2B1.1, and fraud offenses are grouped under 3D1.2(d) with the offense level driven by aggregate loss. Under the 'expanded' relevant-conduct rule of 1B1.3(a)(2), conduct that is part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan as the offense of conviction counts, whether charged or not, and regardless of the district where it occurred. So if the doctor is convicted in either district, the sentencing court can count the false claims made in the other state (all loss, plus the 2B1.1(b)(7) government-program enhancement if applicable), yielding essentially the same range from either court. Loss is the greater of actual or intended loss; Amendment 827 (effective Nov. 1, 2024) moved that rule from commentary into the guideline text, removing the Dupree/Banks-type circuit disagreement about deference to commentary, and for government programs the billed amount is prima facie evidence of intended loss (applied by the Eleventh Circuit); I could not directly verify a Fourth-Circuit-specific difference. (2) Venue limits what each office can charge. Under 3237(a) a continuing/multi-district offense may be prosecuted where begun, continued or completed, but each 1347 execution is generally tried where it was executed; I did not find authority that one district can indict for claims executed solely in the other state (I could not fully research circuit venue law for 1347). Thus each office can safely charge only counts tied to its district, unless a single scheme/execution touches both (e.g., claims submitted from one state to a payer or processor in the other). If either office can validly charge a single scheme spanning both states, the same range would result. (3) Maximum time: each 1347 count carries a 10-year statutory maximum (20/life if serious bodily injury/death). Under 5G1.2(d), if the guideline range exceeds the maximum on the counts of conviction, sentences run consecutively to the extent needed, so the office able to charge the most counts (and bring the most loss within a count-based statutory cap) can produce the highest sentence; that is a function of count number and venue, not district. (4) Splitting prosecutions does not increase time: a second district's sentence for conduct already counted as relevant conduct is governed by 5G1.3(b), which calls for concurrent and adjusted sentences. Conclusion: with the facts given, the best course is a single indictment by whichever office has venue over the larger number of counts / larger share of conduct (likely the district with more executed claims, loss and evidence), with all conduct captured as relevant conduct; absent such a difference, the two offices are equivalent for Guidelines purposes. Unresolved: precise venue law for 1347 in the Fourth and Eleventh Circuits, and any circuit-specific sentencing differences post-Amendment 827.
